meta.title: Learning-Based Reconstruction of Space Resident Objects from Single Orbit Data

abstract: We present a learning-based method, built on the Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) framework, to jointly recover the geometry and appearance of a Space Resident Object (SRO) from a sequence of frames acquired during a single radial boost maneuver. The approach efficiently encodes spatial information while modeling complex, in-the-wild appearance. A key contribution is the explicit separation of geometry and appearance, allowing operational control over visual effects without compromising 3D structure fidelity. A dedicated appearance branch, regularized through learned codes, resolves geometry–appearance ambiguity, preventing illumination variations from being misinterpreted as structural features.

blocks.title: Motivation and Challenges in Satellite Inspection

blocks.html: With space missions increasing the level of autonomy, the need of computing accurate target representation has gained traction in Computer Vision space-related challenges. As a consequence – according to mission-specific requirements – a variety of techniques have been investigated, ranging from minimal 6D representation [1][2] to full geometry reconstruction [3]. In the frame of On- Orbit Servicing, spacecraft 6D pose representation is often preferred over dense geometric reconstruction, especially because the visual perception layer is usually employed to drive rendezvous & docking tools within high-frequency control loops. However, accurate fiducial geometric and photometric representations continue to play a pivotal role in in-space inspection and situational awareness.

Inspection services involve the observation of a Space Resident Object (SRO) with the purpose to survey and analyze its position, configuration, size and shape, and other meaningful features. In [4] several scopes are identified: space situational awareness, non-destructive evaluation, and close (robotic) inspection to mention a few. Among all of them, free-flyer inspectors are typically conceived as dual-use capabilities in both civil and defense scenarios, in which a satellite conducts rendezvous and proximity operations around a target to characterize a space asset. Accordingly, this paper builds on the free-flyer inspection paradigm as a standalone and enabling concept.

To date, inspection initiatives have been primarily driven by institutional missions, such as NASA’s SSPICY [5] and ESA’s e.Inspector [6], while technological advancements are being increasingly pushed by private companies. Most of the architectures developed within these initiatives rely on satellites to collect data, which is subsequently downlinked, allowing 3D reconstruction to be performed on more capable ground-based systems. However, despite the computational advantage of such architectures, several technological challenges remain.
In this paper, we present a free-flyer inspection concept that outperforms conventional reconstruction approaches by proposing solutions to the following challenges:
1. Dual photometric/geometric reconstruction accuracy:

ensuring accurate 3D structure while faithfully modeling appearance is challenging because illumination variations can be mistakenly encoded as geometry, and structural errors can distort surface appearance.

2. Robustness to dynamic lighting conditions: rapid changes in illumination during orbital maneuvers can confuse the reconstruction process. The method must separate intrinsic surface properties from transient lighting to maintain consistent reconstructions.

3. Minimization of the required dataset size: collecting orbital imagery is resource-intensive. Achieving accurate reconstruction from a minimal set of frames enables the inspector satellite to complete acquisition in a single radial-boost maneuver, simplifying GNC operations and reducing propellant consumption.

The inspector satellite is equipped with an RGB camera with 512×512 resolution and performs a radial boost maneuver around the SRO. The acquired frames are downlinked to the ground segment together with associated metadata, including camera intrinsics and extrinsics. A dedicated server then performs reconstruction on the resulting dataset. Finally, the photometric and geometric reconstruction is generated and either delivered to the end user or up-linked to the satellite for use in subsequent servicing operations.

The LEO environment represents the most challenging scenario for assessing the performance of the reconstruction algorithm. In this setting, the target SRO undergoes rapid and extreme variations in illumination, with approximately one-third of the dataset captured during complete eclipse. This scenario was modeled in Blender using a LandSat8 model positioned at an altitude of approximately 500 km. The full orbit of the SRO, including the inspection maneuver, spans about 90 minutes. Furthermore, the inspector satellite is positioned at a distance of 25–50 meters from the target, depending on the phase of the maneuver. Given the orbital altitude and time span, the scenario was simplified by assuming (i) the Earth acts as an inertial reference frame with a constant incoming light direction, and (ii) the SRO follows a circular orbit around the Earth.

Each dataset sample includes (i) a 512×512 RGB frame of the target, (ii) a sequential index indicating the capture order, (iii) the camera intrinsics and extrinsics relative to the SRO, and (iv) a 512×512 depth map of the target.

All components except the last are used during the reconstruction process. The depth map is provided exclusively for quantitative evaluation of the geometric reconstruction and is not used by the reconstruction algorithm.

blocks.html: For more than a decade, image-based 3D reconstruction has been largely driven by Structure-from-Motion and Multi- View Stereo approaches, until the introduction of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [7] representations. Since 2020, the NeRF literature has rapidly expanded, with a large number of variants proposed to address diverse challenges, including improved training efficiency [8], handling unposed datasets [9], and modeling dynamic geometric and appearance properties [10]. Furthermore, several studies have proposed NeRF-based methods specifically tailored to space-related scenarios, including in-Space Situational Awareness [11] and Earth Observation applications [12].

Our reconstruction framework builds upon the NeRF architecture, which represents a 3D scene as a continuous volumetric function. A point x ∈R3 and a viewing direction d ∈S3 are mapped to a density σ(x) and color

To capture high-frequency details, we build upon prior strategies for NeRFs: spatial coordinates are encoded using a multi-resolution hash grid, and view-dependent effects are modeled via spherical harmonics of the viewing direction. Our contribution lies in tailoring the appearance modeling to the challenging conditions of SROs under orbital illumination. We introduce per-frame learnable embeddings that explicitly capture appearance variations across frames, optimized jointly with the network. By decoupling geometry from appearance and leveraging these embeddings, our framework achieves high-fidelity 3D reconstructions while mitigating geometry–appearance ambiguities caused by varying and dynamic illumination.

The training objective is a weighted combination of multiple loss terms. (i) A pixel-wise mean squared error (MSE) enforces photometric consistency between observed frames and rendered images. Standard NeRF regularizers are also applied: (ii) a total variation loss penalizes high-frequency spatial variations in the volumetric representation, reducing grid artifacts and promoting local smoothness, and (iii) a sparsity loss encourages the density field to concentrate on occupied regions by biasing empty space toward zero density. Together, these terms stabilize optimization and foster coherent geometry.

Finally, (iv) we introduce a custom regularization on the per-frame appearance embeddings to encourage smooth transitions. Let ei ∈Rd be the embedding at index i, with Ne total embeddings. The loss is

blocks.html: which minimizes the second-order derivative of the embeddings, ensuring gradual and physically plausible appearance transitions, such as smooth evolution of shadows in satellite imagery.

All results were obtained using a batch size of 4096 rays and an initial learning rate of 0.001, decayed by a factor of 0.9 every 5 epochs. Results are reported for the first 15 epochs of training. All experiments were conducted on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU.
To evaluate the proposed design, a structured experimental campaign was conducted to systematically analyze the sensitivity of the model to key architectural and operational parameters.

A primary computational bottleneck in NeRF–based methods is the number of samples evaluated along each ray during volumetric rendering. This parameter directly impacts both reconstruction fidelity and computational cost. Accordingly, three configurations were investigated, employing 32, 64, and 128 samples per ray, respectively, to quantify the trade-off between rendering accuracy and processing burden.

The capability to capture dynamic appearance variations is governed by the dimensionality of the appearance latent code. To assess its influence on representation capacity and generalization, three alternative dimensions were considered: 4, 8, and 16. This analysis enabled evaluation of the balance between expressive power and model complexity. Results are reported in Table 1.

Another critical factor, particularly relevant to mission operations and onboard data budgets, is the number of input frames required to achieve satisfactory threedimensional reconstruction quality. To examine this dependency, three datasets with different angular sampling resolutions were constructed: (i) 4° spacing (90 frames), (ii) 3° spacing (120 frames), and (iii) 2° spacing (180 frames). To isolate the effect of dataset density while containing computational cost, these experiments were performed using a baseline configuration with 32 samples per ray and an appearance code dimension of 4. Results are provided in Table 2.

blocks.html: We further assess the quality of the photometric reconstruction through a qualitative analysis of appearance interpolation. Specifically, we render the same scene while continuously interpolating the appearance embeddings between two reference extrema, and evaluate the naturalness and smoothness of the resulting visual transitions. This analysis allows us to verify that the model produces coherent and gradual photometric changes without introducing visual artifacts. An example of this transition is shown in Figure 2.

blocks.html: Based on the results of both the geometric and photometric evaluations — particularly those reported in Table 1 — the dominant factor affecting performance is the sampling density along each ray. In contrast, the dimensionality of the appearance embeddings has a negligible impact on reconstruction accuracy. Nevertheless, it plays a crucial role in disentangling geometry from appearance effects and in enabling explicit control over the rendered appearance.

The adoption of a multi-resolution hash embedding substantially enhances the representation of high-frequency image components, yielding sharper reconstructions and improved fidelity in fine structures, such as slender tubular elements and planar surfaces. Furthermore, the introduction of segmentation significantly improves background quality by isolating the SRO from the surrounding scene and reducing sparse artifacts. This effect is illustrated in Figure 3.

Regarding the dataset size, Table 2 highlights a key advantage of the proposed approach, namely its ability to significantly reduce the amount of data required for accurate reconstruction. This characteristic makes NeRF-based architectures particularly attractive when compared to data-intensive pipelines.
From an operational standpoint, several challenges must be addressed before the approach can be deployed in a service environment.

A primary limitation is the dependence of NeRF-based methods on accurate camera odometry. During radial boost maneuvers around the SRO, pose estimates may degrade, introducing inconsistencies in the reconstructed radiance field. Joint optimization of camera poses and scene representation, as in frameworks such as iNeRF [13], could improve robustness under imperfect navigation data.

A second challenge concerns sampling along each ray. Reconstruction quality is highly sensitive to sampling density, and at large distances even hundreds of samples per ray may be insufficient or computationally costly. Rescaling odometry within a bounded spatial domain can increase effective sampling resolution without adding significant overhead, and adaptive or normalized scene representations warrant further study.

Finally, operational deployment requires reliable fore-ground–background segmentation. Gains from supervised segmentation must translate into a concrete ability to isolate the SRO, even with arbitrary geometry or imperfect masks. System robustness under blurred or artifact-prone segmentation remains an open question.
Addressing these issues is essential to move from proofof-concept to a fully operational and reliable service.
